    Migrating from Prophet to skforecast¶

    Prophet made forecasting accessible to many Python users: one model with trend, seasonality and holidays, fitted in a few lines. As of version 1.4.0, Prophet is in maintenance mode: it accepts bug fixes and dependency updates, but no new features are planned.

    This guide is for users who have Prophet code, or follow tutorials based on it, and want to try skforecast. It covers:

    • How each Prophet concept translates to skforecast.

    • Two side-by-side backtests with the same folds for both libraries: the daily series of Prophet's own quick start, and an hourly series with exogenous variables.

    • When Prophet is still a reasonable choice and what skforecast adds.

    Prophet concepts in skforecast¶

    Prophet skforecast
    DataFrame with ds and y columns pandas Series with a DatetimeIndex and a frequency
    Prophet() and fit(df) ForecasterRecursive(estimator, lags) and fit(y, exog)
    make_future_dataframe(periods=h) and predict(future) predict(steps=h): future dates are created internally
    Trend (piecewise linear with changepoints) Autoregressive lags follow the level of the series; differentiation=1 for series with a strong trend
    yearly_seasonality, weekly_seasonality, add_seasonality(fourier_order=...) Fourier terms as exogenous variables, or calendar_features=CalendarFeatures(...), plus seasonal lags (for example 7 or 168)
    add_seasonality(condition_name=...) Tree-based models learn the interactions between calendar features and exogenous variables
    holidays table with lower_window and upper_window Binary columns in exog that cover the same days, or calculate_distance_from_holiday
    add_regressor(name) A column in exog
    interval_width=0.8 (yhat_lower, yhat_upper) predict_interval(steps, interval=0.8) (lower_bound, upper_bound)
    cross_validation(model, initial, period, horizon) backtesting_forecaster(forecaster, y, cv=TimeSeriesFold(initial_train_size, steps, refit))
    performance_metrics(df_cv) metric argument of backtesting_forecaster
    growth='logistic' with cap and floor No direct equivalent; to keep predictions within bounds, transform the series with transformer_y

    The estimator can be any scikit-learn compatible regressor: a linear model such as Ridge is the closest translation of Prophet (a linear model of trend, Fourier terms and holidays), while gradient boosting models such as LightGBM capture non-linear effects and interactions.

    Case 1: daily series with yearly seasonality¶

    The series is the log of the daily views of the Wikipedia page of Peyton Manning, the dataset of Prophet's quick start. It has a strong yearly seasonality (the NFL season) and peaks during the playoffs and the Super Bowl.

    Prophet ignores the dates without data, while skforecast needs a complete index. To compare both libraries on the same data, the missing values are interpolated.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    # Data
# ==============================================================================
data = fetch_dataset('wikipedia_visits')
data['y'] = data['y'].interpolate()

# Plot
# ==============================================================================
set_dark_theme()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
data['y'].plot(ax=ax)
ax.set_title('Log daily views of the Wikipedia page of Peyton Manning')
ax.set_xlabel('');
    # Data # ============================================================================== data = fetch_dataset('wikipedia_visits') data['y'] = data['y'].interpolate() # Plot # ============================================================================== set_dark_theme() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3)) data['y'].plot(ax=ax) ax.set_title('Log daily views of the Wikipedia page of Peyton Manning') ax.set_xlabel('');

    Holidays¶

    Prophet takes a table of holidays with a window of days around each one. In skforecast, holidays are exogenous variables: one binary column per type of holiday that marks the same days. The playoff and Super Bowl dates are those of Prophet's documentation, with upper_window=1 (the game day and the day after).

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    # Holidays: Prophet table and skforecast exogenous variables
# ==============================================================================
playoffs = pd.to_datetime([
    '2008-01-13', '2009-01-03', '2010-01-16', '2010-01-24', '2010-02-07',
    '2011-01-08', '2013-01-12', '2014-01-12', '2014-01-19', '2014-02-02',
    '2015-01-11', '2016-01-17', '2016-01-24', '2016-02-07'
])
superbowls = pd.to_datetime(['2010-02-07', '2014-02-02', '2016-02-07'])

holidays = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({'holiday': 'playoff', 'ds': playoffs, 'lower_window': 0, 'upper_window': 1}),
    pd.DataFrame({'holiday': 'superbowl', 'ds': superbowls, 'lower_window': 0, 'upper_window': 1}),
])

exog = pd.DataFrame(index=data.index)
exog['playoff'] = data.index.isin(playoffs.union(playoffs.shift(1, freq='D'))).astype(int)
exog['superbowl'] = data.index.isin(superbowls.union(superbowls.shift(1, freq='D'))).astype(int)
    # Holidays: Prophet table and skforecast exogenous variables # ============================================================================== playoffs = pd.to_datetime([ '2008-01-13', '2009-01-03', '2010-01-16', '2010-01-24', '2010-02-07', '2011-01-08', '2013-01-12', '2014-01-12', '2014-01-19', '2014-02-02', '2015-01-11', '2016-01-17', '2016-01-24', '2016-02-07' ]) superbowls = pd.to_datetime(['2010-02-07', '2014-02-02', '2016-02-07']) holidays = pd.concat([ pd.DataFrame({'holiday': 'playoff', 'ds': playoffs, 'lower_window': 0, 'upper_window': 1}), pd.DataFrame({'holiday': 'superbowl', 'ds': superbowls, 'lower_window': 0, 'upper_window': 1}), ]) exog = pd.DataFrame(index=data.index) exog['playoff'] = data.index.isin(playoffs.union(playoffs.shift(1, freq='D'))).astype(int) exog['superbowl'] = data.index.isin(superbowls.union(superbowls.shift(1, freq='D'))).astype(int)

    Seasonality¶

    By default, Prophet models the yearly seasonality with 10 pairs of Fourier terms and the weekly seasonality with 3. The same terms, added as exogenous variables, give a linear model the same seasonal shapes. CalendarFeatures creates calendar features from the index without building exog: one pair of sine and cosine terms per feature with encoding='cyclical', or the raw values (hour, day of the week...), which suit tree-based models (Case 2).

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    # Fourier terms with the same periods and orders as Prophet's defaults
# ==============================================================================
t = (data.index - pd.Timestamp('1970-01-01')).days.to_numpy()
for name, period, order in [('yearly', 365.25, 10), ('weekly', 7, 3)]:
    for k in range(1, order + 1):
        exog[f'{name}_sin_{k}'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * t / period)
        exog[f'{name}_cos_{k}'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * t / period)

exog.head(3)
    # Fourier terms with the same periods and orders as Prophet's defaults # ============================================================================== t = (data.index - pd.Timestamp('1970-01-01')).days.to_numpy() for name, period, order in [('yearly', 365.25, 10), ('weekly', 7, 3)]: for k in range(1, order + 1): exog[f'{name}_sin_{k}'] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * k * t / period) exog[f'{name}_cos_{k}'] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * k * t / period) exog.head(3)

    Fit and predict¶

    Both models forecast the last 30 days. Prophet needs a DataFrame with the future dates, created with make_future_dataframe. skforecast only needs the number of steps (and the exogenous variables of those dates). The forecaster combines the last 14 values of the series (lags) with the holidays and the Fourier terms in a Ridge regression.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    # Prophet: fit and predict the last 30 days
# ==============================================================================
steps = 30
df = data.reset_index().rename(columns={'date': 'ds'})

model = Prophet(holidays=holidays)
model.fit(df.iloc[:-steps])
future = model.make_future_dataframe(periods=steps)
forecast = model.predict(future)
predictions_prophet = (
    forecast.set_index('ds')[['yhat', 'yhat_lower', 'yhat_upper']].iloc[-steps:]
)
predictions_prophet.head(3)
    # Prophet: fit and predict the last 30 days # ============================================================================== steps = 30 df = data.reset_index().rename(columns={'date': 'ds'}) model = Prophet(holidays=holidays) model.fit(df.iloc[:-steps]) future = model.make_future_dataframe(periods=steps) forecast = model.predict(future) predictions_prophet = ( forecast.set_index('ds')[['yhat', 'yhat_lower', 'yhat_upper']].iloc[-steps:] ) predictions_prophet.head(3)
    Out[5]:
    yhat yhat_lower yhat_upper
    ds
    2015-12-22 8.080191 7.529004 8.700969
    2015-12-23 7.904629 7.291213 8.483937
    2015-12-24 7.904908 7.327653 8.479225
    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    # skforecast: fit and predict the last 30 days
# ==============================================================================
forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(estimator=Ridge(), lags=14)
forecaster.fit(
    y                         = data['y'].iloc[:-steps],
    exog                      = exog.iloc[:-steps],
    store_in_sample_residuals = True
)
predictions = forecaster.predict_interval(
                  steps    = steps,
                  exog     = exog.iloc[-steps:],
                  interval = 0.8
              )
predictions.head(3)
    # skforecast: fit and predict the last 30 days # ============================================================================== forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(estimator=Ridge(), lags=14) forecaster.fit( y = data['y'].iloc[:-steps], exog = exog.iloc[:-steps], store_in_sample_residuals = True ) predictions = forecaster.predict_interval( steps = steps, exog = exog.iloc[-steps:], interval = 0.8 ) predictions.head(3)
    Out[6]:
    pred lower_bound upper_bound
    2015-12-22 8.167202 7.806039 8.487544
    2015-12-23 7.964266 7.585161 8.234653
    2015-12-24 7.969479 7.545609 8.304264

    Both libraries return an 80% prediction interval. In skforecast, its coverage depends on the residuals used to build it; the probabilistic forecasting guides explain how to calibrate it.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    # Plot predictions
# ==============================================================================
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
data['y'].iloc[-120:].plot(ax=ax, label='observed', color='gray')
predictions_prophet['yhat'].plot(ax=ax, label='Prophet')
predictions['pred'].plot(ax=ax, label='skforecast (Ridge)')
ax.set_title('Forecast of the last 30 days')
ax.set_xlabel('')
ax.legend();
    # Plot predictions # ============================================================================== fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3)) data['y'].iloc[-120:].plot(ax=ax, label='observed', color='gray') predictions_prophet['yhat'].plot(ax=ax, label='Prophet') predictions['pred'].plot(ax=ax, label='skforecast (Ridge)') ax.set_title('Forecast of the last 30 days') ax.set_xlabel('') ax.legend();

    Backtesting with the same folds¶

    Prophet's cross_validation and skforecast's backtesting_forecaster work the same way: they refit the model at each cutoff and forecast the next horizon (steps) periods. To compare both libraries on exactly the same folds, the cutoffs passed to Prophet are the last training dates of the folds of TimeSeriesFold: 24 folds of 30 days over the last two years, with an expanding training window (fixed_train_size=False), as Prophet does.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    # Folds shared by both libraries
# ==============================================================================
cv = TimeSeriesFold(
         steps              = 30,
         initial_train_size = len(data) - 720,
         refit              = True,
         fixed_train_size   = False,
         verbose            = False
     )

# Prophet cutoffs: the last training date of each fold of `cv`
cutoffs = pd.date_range(end=data.index[-31], periods=24, freq='30D')
print(f"Number of folds : {len(cutoffs)}")
print(f"First cutoff    : {cutoffs[0].date()}")
print(f"Last cutoff     : {cutoffs[-1].date()}")
    # Folds shared by both libraries # ============================================================================== cv = TimeSeriesFold( steps = 30, initial_train_size = len(data) - 720, refit = True, fixed_train_size = False, verbose = False ) # Prophet cutoffs: the last training date of each fold of `cv` cutoffs = pd.date_range(end=data.index[-31], periods=24, freq='30D') print(f"Number of folds : {len(cutoffs)}") print(f"First cutoff : {cutoffs[0].date()}") print(f"Last cutoff : {cutoffs[-1].date()}")
    Number of folds : 24
First cutoff    : 2014-01-30
Last cutoff     : 2015-12-21
    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    # Prophet: cross-validation
# ==============================================================================
# cross_validation takes a fitted model and refits a copy of it at each cutoff
model = Prophet(holidays=holidays).fit(df)

start = time.perf_counter()
cv_prophet = cross_validation(model, cutoffs=list(cutoffs), horizon='30 days', disable_tqdm=True)
time_prophet = time.perf_counter() - start
    # Prophet: cross-validation # ============================================================================== # cross_validation takes a fitted model and refits a copy of it at each cutoff model = Prophet(holidays=holidays).fit(df) start = time.perf_counter() cv_prophet = cross_validation(model, cutoffs=list(cutoffs), horizon='30 days', disable_tqdm=True) time_prophet = time.perf_counter() - start
    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    # skforecast: backtesting of the Ridge forecaster and of a baseline
# ==============================================================================
start = time.perf_counter()
metric_ridge, predictions_ridge = backtesting_forecaster(
                                      forecaster    = ForecasterRecursive(estimator=Ridge(), lags=14),
                                      y             = data['y'],
                                      exog          = exog,
                                      cv            = cv,
                                      metric        = 'mean_absolute_error',
                                      show_progress = False
                                  )
time_ridge = time.perf_counter() - start

# Baseline: the value of the same day of the previous week
metric_baseline, _ = backtesting_forecaster(
                         forecaster    = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=pd.DateOffset(days=7)),
                         y             = data['y'],
                         cv            = cv,
                         metric        = 'mean_absolute_error',
                         show_progress = False
                     )
    # skforecast: backtesting of the Ridge forecaster and of a baseline # ============================================================================== start = time.perf_counter() metric_ridge, predictions_ridge = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(estimator=Ridge(), lags=14), y = data['y'], exog = exog, cv = cv, metric = 'mean_absolute_error', show_progress = False ) time_ridge = time.perf_counter() - start # Baseline: the value of the same day of the previous week metric_baseline, _ = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=pd.DateOffset(days=7)), y = data['y'], cv = cv, metric = 'mean_absolute_error', show_progress = False )
    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    # Results
# ==============================================================================
results = pd.DataFrame({
    'model': ['Prophet', 'skforecast (Ridge)', 'Baseline (same day of the previous week)'],
    'mae': [
        mean_absolute_error(cv_prophet['y'], cv_prophet['yhat']),
        metric_ridge.at[0, 'mean_absolute_error'],
        metric_baseline.at[0, 'mean_absolute_error'],
    ],
    'time (s)': [time_prophet, time_ridge, np.nan],
})
results.round(3)
    # Results # ============================================================================== results = pd.DataFrame({ 'model': ['Prophet', 'skforecast (Ridge)', 'Baseline (same day of the previous week)'], 'mae': [ mean_absolute_error(cv_prophet['y'], cv_prophet['yhat']), metric_ridge.at[0, 'mean_absolute_error'], metric_baseline.at[0, 'mean_absolute_error'], ], 'time (s)': [time_prophet, time_ridge, np.nan], }) results.round(3)
    Out[11]:
    model mae time (s)
    0 Prophet 0.333 17.072
    1 skforecast (Ridge) 0.348 0.177
    2 Baseline (same day of the previous week) 0.481 NaN

    On Prophet's own quick start series, Prophet has the lowest error: its MAE is about 4% lower than that of the Ridge forecaster, and both are well ahead of the baseline. This is the kind of series Prophet was designed for: daily, with a strong and stable yearly seasonality and known events. The skforecast model, with the same seasonalities and holidays as Prophet plus lags instead of a trend, runs the 24 folds about 100 times faster.

    Case 2: hourly series with exogenous variables¶

    The series is the hourly number of users of the bike sharing system of Washington D.C. (2011 and 2012), with the weather and the type of day as exogenous variables. The daily pattern of a working day (two commuting peaks) differs from that of a weekend or holiday.

    Both models forecast the next 7 days (168 hours) in 8 folds over the last 8 weeks. Both receive the observed weather of the forecast horizon; in production, weather forecasts would add error to both.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    # Data
# ==============================================================================
data_bike = fetch_dataset('bike_sharing')
exog_cols = ['temp', 'hum', 'windspeed', 'holiday', 'workingday']
y_bike = data_bike['users']
exog_bike = data_bike[exog_cols]

# Folds shared by both libraries
# ==============================================================================
cv_bike = TimeSeriesFold(
              steps              = 168,
              initial_train_size = len(data_bike) - 168 * 8,
              refit              = True,
              fixed_train_size   = False,
              verbose            = False
          )

# Prophet cutoffs: the last training date of each fold of `cv_bike`
cutoffs_bike = pd.date_range(end=data_bike.index[-169], periods=8, freq='168h')
    # Data # ============================================================================== data_bike = fetch_dataset('bike_sharing') exog_cols = ['temp', 'hum', 'windspeed', 'holiday', 'workingday'] y_bike = data_bike['users'] exog_bike = data_bike[exog_cols] # Folds shared by both libraries # ============================================================================== cv_bike = TimeSeriesFold( steps = 168, initial_train_size = len(data_bike) - 168 * 8, refit = True, fixed_train_size = False, verbose = False ) # Prophet cutoffs: the last training date of each fold of `cv_bike` cutoffs_bike = pd.date_range(end=data_bike.index[-169], periods=8, freq='168h')

╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

    For Prophet, the configuration follows its documentation: weather and type of day with add_regressor, and a conditional daily seasonality, one for working days and another for the rest, so that each type of day has its own daily pattern. The Fourier order of these seasonalities (6) is higher than the default of the daily seasonality (4) to capture the two commuting peaks.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    # Prophet: regressors and conditional daily seasonality
# ==============================================================================
df_bike = (
    data_bike[['users'] + exog_cols]
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={'date_time': 'ds', 'users': 'y'})
)
df_bike['workday'] = df_bike['workingday'] == 1
df_bike['offday'] = ~df_bike['workday']

model = Prophet(daily_seasonality=False)
model.add_seasonality(name='daily_workday', period=1, fourier_order=6, condition_name='workday')
model.add_seasonality(name='daily_offday', period=1, fourier_order=6, condition_name='offday')
for col in exog_cols:
    model.add_regressor(col)
model.fit(df_bike)  # cross_validation refits a copy at each cutoff

start = time.perf_counter()
cv_prophet_bike = cross_validation(
                      model, cutoffs=list(cutoffs_bike), horizon='168 hours', disable_tqdm=True
                  )
time_prophet_bike = time.perf_counter() - start
    # Prophet: regressors and conditional daily seasonality # ============================================================================== df_bike = ( data_bike[['users'] + exog_cols] .reset_index() .rename(columns={'date_time': 'ds', 'users': 'y'}) ) df_bike['workday'] = df_bike['workingday'] == 1 df_bike['offday'] = ~df_bike['workday'] model = Prophet(daily_seasonality=False) model.add_seasonality(name='daily_workday', period=1, fourier_order=6, condition_name='workday') model.add_seasonality(name='daily_offday', period=1, fourier_order=6, condition_name='offday') for col in exog_cols: model.add_regressor(col) model.fit(df_bike) # cross_validation refits a copy at each cutoff start = time.perf_counter() cv_prophet_bike = cross_validation( model, cutoffs=list(cutoffs_bike), horizon='168 hours', disable_tqdm=True ) time_prophet_bike = time.perf_counter() - start

    In skforecast, the forecaster is a LightGBM model with lags (the last 3 hours, and the same hour of the previous day and of the previous week with the hours around it), calendar features (hour, day of the week and month) and the same exogenous variables. The trees learn from the data that the effect of the hour depends on the type of day.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    # skforecast: LightGBM with lags, calendar features and exogenous variables
# ==============================================================================
forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(
                 estimator         = LGBMRegressor(random_state=123, verbose=-1),
                 lags              = [1, 2, 3, 23, 24, 25, 167, 168, 169],
                 calendar_features = CalendarFeatures(
                                         features = ['hour', 'day_of_week', 'month'],
                                         encoding = None
                                     )
             )

start = time.perf_counter()
metric_lgbm, predictions_lgbm = backtesting_forecaster(
                                    forecaster    = forecaster,
                                    y             = y_bike,
                                    exog          = exog_bike,
                                    cv            = cv_bike,
                                    metric        = 'mean_absolute_error',
                                    show_progress = False
                                )
time_lgbm = time.perf_counter() - start

# Baseline: the value of the same hour of the previous week
metric_baseline_bike, _ = backtesting_forecaster(
                              forecaster    = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=pd.DateOffset(days=7)),
                              y             = y_bike,
                              cv            = cv_bike,
                              metric        = 'mean_absolute_error',
                              show_progress = False
                          )
    # skforecast: LightGBM with lags, calendar features and exogenous variables # ============================================================================== forecaster = ForecasterRecursive( estimator = LGBMRegressor(random_state=123, verbose=-1), lags = [1, 2, 3, 23, 24, 25, 167, 168, 169], calendar_features = CalendarFeatures( features = ['hour', 'day_of_week', 'month'], encoding = None ) ) start = time.perf_counter() metric_lgbm, predictions_lgbm = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = forecaster, y = y_bike, exog = exog_bike, cv = cv_bike, metric = 'mean_absolute_error', show_progress = False ) time_lgbm = time.perf_counter() - start # Baseline: the value of the same hour of the previous week metric_baseline_bike, _ = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=pd.DateOffset(days=7)), y = y_bike, cv = cv_bike, metric = 'mean_absolute_error', show_progress = False )

    On this series, the LightGBM forecaster has an error about 8% lower than that of Prophet and runs the 8 folds about 30 times faster, without having to specify which seasonalities depend on the type of day. In the week of the plot, the daily peak predicted by Prophet falls short of the observed one every day, while the LightGBM forecaster gets closer to it on most days.

    Neither model was tuned beyond the configuration shown, and two series are not a general benchmark: the point is that the best option depends on the series, and backtesting both on the same folds is how to choose.

    When to keep Prophet and what skforecast adds¶

    Prophet is still a reasonable choice for a single daily or weekly series with a strong and stable seasonality and known events (as in Case 1), especially when the forecast has to be explained as the sum of a trend, seasonalities and holiday effects.

    skforecast adds the most when:

    • The series depends on exogenous variables or on interactions between patterns (as in Case 2): any scikit-learn compatible regressor, such as LightGBM, learns them from the data.

    • There are many series: a global model learns from all of them at once, instead of one Prophet model per series.

    • Models have to be refitted many times, in backtesting, hyperparameter search or production: training is much faster.

    • You want to compare model families with the same API and the same backtesting: machine learning, statistical models (ARIMA, ETS) and foundation models that forecast without training.

    Next steps¶

    • Calendar features and exogenous variables: the skforecast counterparts of seasonalities, holidays and regressors.

    • Backtesting: all the options of TimeSeriesFold, such as gaps, fixed training windows or refitting every n folds.

    • Probabilistic forecasting: bootstrapping, conformal prediction and quantile regression.

    • Forecasters: all the forecasters of skforecast, from machine learning to statistical, foundation and deep learning models, with the same API.
